D.6 Two-dimensional J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} square-lattice experiment

Using the same method hyper-parameters as above, we evaluate PWO on the frustrated spin-1/21/2 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on a two-dimensional square lattice,

H^J1​–​J22​D=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j,\displaystyle\hat{H}_{J_{1}\text{--}J_{2}}^{\mathrm{2D}}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}, (123)

where ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle and ⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle denote nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, respectively. We use an L×LL\times L square lattice with L=10L=10, periodic boundary conditions, J1=1J_{1}=1, and J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5. All runs are restricted to the zero-magnetization sector, Stotz=0S^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}=0, by masking infeasible autoregressive choices during sampling and evaluation.

For this experiment we use a complex-valued patch-autoregressive transformer designed for two-dimensional lattices. Instead of generating spins one at a time, the model partitions the 10×1010\times 10 lattice into non-overlapping 2×22\times 2 patches. Each patch is represented as a categorical token with vocabulary size 24=162^{4}=16, so the full configuration is generated as a sequence of

T=(L2)2=25\displaystyle T=\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)^{2}=25 (124)

autoregressive tokens. The wavefunction is factorized over patch tokens as

log⁡ψθ​(𝐬)=∑t=1T[12​log⁡pθ​(at∣a<t)+i​ϕθ​(at∣a<t)],\displaystyle\log\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\frac{1}{2}\log p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid a_{<t})+i\,\phi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid a_{<t})\right], (125)

where the factor 1/21/2 corresponds to the Born-rule convention Pθ​(𝐬)=|ψθ​(𝐬)|2P_{\theta}(\mathbf{s})=|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{s})|^{2}.

The model prepends a beginning-of-sequence token and embeds patch tokens with learned token embeddings of dimension 6464. We also use learned site embeddings and prefix-count features that encode the partial magnetization constraint. These embeddings are projected to width 9696, normalized with layer normalization, and passed through an 88-layer causal transformer backbone. Each transformer block uses 66 attention heads, two-dimensional axial RoPE with base 100100, residual connections, and a feedforward width of 4×96=3844\times 96=384.

From the final transformer representation, the model uses separate amplitude and phase heads. Both heads are two-layer MLPs with hidden dimension 192192 and GELU activations. The amplitude head outputs masked conditional log-probabilities through a log-softmax, ensuring exact normalization over feasible patch choices. The phase head outputs centered phase increments using a π​tanh⁡(⋅)\pi\tanh(\cdot) parameterization, with small initialization scale 10−310^{-3}. This gives an exactly sampleable complex autoregressive neural quantum state adapted to the two-dimensional square lattice.

While the aim of this experiment is to compare optimizers and not to achieve the state-of-the-art variational energy (around -199.0536 [Rende et al., 2024]), we note that the energy of the PWO-trained autoregressive transformer of 1.5M parameters is −185-185 after 30 mins, reaches −195.6-195.6 after 24 hours, and keeps decreasing. The run is on a single GPU and imposes no symmetries, except for zero-magnetization sampling.

D.7 Scaling Experiment

To study how performance scales with model capacity, we train three model sizes on the frustrated Heisenberg J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chain (N=12N=12, J1=1J_{1}=1, J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, periodic boundary conditions) using PWO, Adam, and minSR. All three sizes share the same autoregressive GRU architecture described in Appendix D.2; they differ only in the number of recurrent layers and hidden dimensions. Table 7 summarises the sizes and the corresponding total parameter counts.

The hyperparameters used for each optimization method in the scaling experiment are listed in Table 8. The schedule and clipping parameters are identical to those of the main J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} experiments (see Tables 5 and 2); only the number of transition steps differs to account for the change in model size.
